talk.title: An AI Manifesto
talk.thesis: Intent is the new oil. Capping tokens is the leak.
talk.speaker: Brad Baker

slides.title: Intent is the new oil. Capping tokens is the leak.
meta: 30 minutes · one vote at the end
slides.notes: Thanks for having me. This is a talk for the people in the building who already get it — the AI leads, the builders, the ones who've watched a demo turn into a waitlist. I'm going to give you the state of the market in a handful of machines, and then I'm going to give you the words to take upstairs, because the people who sign the cheques are not seeing what you're seeing. At the end, you vote.

slides.title: “My company spent my entire 2026 budget in Q1. Can you make this more efficient?”
slides.cite: A client complaint Sam Altman quoted on stage, June 2026. He called token costs “a huge issue” that “never came up” six months earlier.
slides.notes: This isn't me. This is the vendor's own CEO, on stage in June, quoting a customer. Six months earlier nobody asked this question. Now it's the question. Hands up if you've had a version of this conversation with your CFO this year. [pause] Keep your hand up if the answer you got was "cap it." That's the room I'm talking to. Altman's answer is efficiency. Mine is ownership. Here's why.

slides.title: The ask: fund owned capacity for your heaviest users, not more seats.

cols.v: Demand outruns price. The bill detonates in the quarters you're winning.
Cap your best people and they route around you — through a door the contract doesn't cover.
Three rungs you own, one gate you rent. Volume uncapped; judgment escalates.

lead.v: Capacity, not subscriptions — one refresh at a time.

slides.notes: Answer first, so you can check my working. The ask you take upstairs is: fund owned capacity for the people who burn the most, instead of buying more seats and capping them. Three things get you there. The meter: demand is outrunning price, and that's a finance problem, not a technology problem. The leak: when you cap, your best people don't stop, they go personal. The ladder: the architecture that fixes both. Then we'll write the three sentences for your CFO, CIO and CEO.

slides.title: Token demand rose a millionfold; the price fell sixteenfold. The bill is the problem.

stats.l: frontier list price per million tokens ($60 → $3.85)

slides.source: Altman on stage, June 2026 (volume); 2020 API launch pricing and Artificial Analysis (price); log-interpolated.
slides.notes: This is a meter, not a chart. The needle is tokens a month on a log dial — one big tick for every ten times more. Watch it go from 2019 to 2026. [advance] A millionfold. Now look at the tariff carriage on the right — the price per million. It barely moves: sixty dollars down to three eighty-five. That's the whole story. Everybody tells your CFO tokens are getting cheaper, and for yesterday's capability they are — nine to nine hundred times a year. But the price of the best model stays in the same band, and usage grows faster than prices fall. The bill went up sixty-four thousand times. And you can type your own number in the box — try it later with your own monthly burn.

slides.title: One three-person team burned 603 billion tokens in a month.
slides.aside: That team is not a cautionary tale. That team is who you're looking for inside your own walls.
slides.source: OpenClaw creator Peter Steinberger's published monthly bill (Tom's Hardware).
slides.notes: Here's the other end of the meter. Three people, about a hundred coding agents, six hundred and three billion tokens, one point three million dollars, one month. The finance reflex is to treat that as the horror story. I want you to treat it as the recruiting brief. That's what a native looks like at full speed. You have people like that, or you have people who would be like that if you let them. Remember them — they come back in ten minutes.

slides.title: Every flat plan dies the same way: hooked first, metered second.

example.l: users in 45 days at one large agency — then rationing, because small jobs by hundreds of thousands of people “get expensive real, real fast.”

slides.source: Usage-limit changes, 2026; AI Weekly, Aug 2026 (the agency rollout).
slides.notes: You've all lived this as consumers. The flat plan gets you hooked. Then the five-hour session cap. Then the weekly cap. Then the overflow — pay as you go. The enterprise version is the same arc with a bigger number on it. One large agency went from zero to nineteen thousand users in forty-five days on per-token billing. Then they rationed. Not because it didn't work — because it worked. That's what I call the budget detonation: last year the AI line was a subscription anyone could forecast. This year it's a meter wired to how hard your best people work, and it goes off in exactly the quarters you're winning. A CFO can live with a big number. A CFO cannot live with a number that detonates.

slides.title: The median business spends $137 a person a year on AI. The best spend half a salary.

stats.l: median business, per employee a year
top 1% of businesses, growing ~14% a month
Jensen Huang's bar for a $500K engineer — half the salary

slides.source: Ramp AI Index, June 2026 (70,000+ US businesses, annualized); Huang on the record (Tom's Hardware).
slides.notes: So what's a sane number? For the first time the industry has benchmarks, and the spread is the story. This is a steelyard — a weighing beam on a log scale. The poise is what the median business spends per person a year on AI: a hundred and thirty-seven dollars. [advance] The top one percent: eighty-nine thousand, growing fourteen percent a month. [advance] And Jensen Huang, on the record: if a five-hundred-thousand-dollar engineer doesn't consume at least two hundred and fifty thousand in tokens, he's "deeply alarmed." Half the salary. Only then does the beam level. If your number is closer to a hundred and thirty-seven than to ten or twenty-five percent of salary, your natives are already routing around you.

slides.title: Models could do 94% of the tasks in computing jobs. We let them do a third.
slides.source: Massenkoff & McCrory, “Labor market impacts of AI,” Anthropic, 5 March 2026.
slides.notes: Spend is one way to see the gap. Work is the other. In March, Anthropic published two numbers per occupation: what share of tasks a model could theoretically do, and what share it's observed actually doing at work. For computer and math jobs: could, ninety-four percent. [advance] Does: thirty-three. [advance] The sixty-one points in between are not a capability problem. Look at what's holding the warp: a clamp, a coin box and a padlock. Permission, plumbing, and the meter. That's the exact shape of what a capped organization leaves on the table — and it's the most fundable sentence in this talk.

slides.title: Cap your natives and they leave by the side door the contract doesn't cover.

stats.l: of office workers used AI tools they believed weren't allowed
believe leadership plays by different rules

slides.notes: Here's what happens to the natives when the meter arrives. The front door is your enterprise contract — metered turnstile, not trained on. [advance] You cap it. The bar drops. The work doesn't stop; it backs up. [advance] And then it goes out the side door — personal accounts. Sixty-six percent of office workers have used AI tools they believed weren't allowed. Eighty-eight percent have shared work information through them. And notice who's nearest the side door: executives use shadow AI the most. Eighty-one percent of workers think leadership plays by different rules. They're right.

slides.title: The contract protects the front door. The training toggle lives at the side door.
head: Enterprise · API · government
Consumer plans
rows: A toggle in the user's settings
Five years, if the toggle is on
slides.line: What leaks isn't customer data. It's how you work: which tools, which decisions, which features you're building next.
slides.source: Anthropic consumer terms (Aug 2025) and commercial terms; equivalent terms at every major lab.
slides.notes: Read the terms carefully and you'll see what they protect: the traffic that goes through the enterprise. Enterprise, API and government traffic is excluded from training at every major lab. The consumer plans — the ones two-thirds of your workforce are quietly using — are where the training toggle lives, with five-year retention if it's on. And here's the part people miss: what flows out isn't customer data. Stealing that would be suicide for a lab. It's how you work. The early leak is a leader thinking a product through before a dollar is committed. The lucrative leak is later: the features and fixes you ship through their model.

slides.title: The labs ship where the usage map is dense: images, code, security, finance, legal.
slides.source: Public product launches, in order; Anthropic Economic Index (30+ categories); Artificial Analysis index 38 vs 61. Heights illustrative; the causal reading is Brad's.
slides.notes: The labs say this part out loud. Anthropic publishes an Economic Index built by classifying millions of conversations into more than thirty categories of work. That's the usage map — this table. [advance] Image generation, 2022. [advance] Software — the coding agents. [advance] Security. [advance] Finance, a whole CFO stack. [advance] Legal. Each one a capability spike dropped exactly where the map was dense. Nobody is alleging a lab lifted a feature from a customer — the mechanism is aggregate, by their own published method. The two glass planes are real scores: the best US open model at 38 runs on your own iron, uncapped; the frontier at 61, metered. Most of the field sits under the open plane. [advance] And the dashed cell is the question for your board: is yours next? Three conditions: the routine eighty percent is text and judgment, the market is big enough, and your category is in their top thirty.

slides.title: Capping tokens starts an eight-step loop. Owned capacity breaks it at step three.
slides.source: PagerDuty, June 2026; AI Weekly, Aug 2026; Anthropic consumer terms, Aug 2025; Anthropic Economic Index.
slides.notes: Put it together and you get a loop — and every step is already happening somewhere. One: usage explodes. [advance] Two: the meter arrives. [advance] Three: you cap the natives, because rationing is how a CFO survives a meter. [advance] Four: they go personal. [advance] Five: personal accounts train. [advance] Six: intent becomes their roadmap. [advance] Seven: the spike eats the eighty percent — the routine work of your industry ships as someone else's near-free feature. [advance] Eight is the only step you control. You can't set their prices or what a consumer account trains on. You control whether you cap your own people. Owned, uncapped capacity throws the switch at step three, and steps four through seven never happen.

slides.title: The best US open model is a third less smart, 6.6× cheaper and twice as fast.
slides.line: Run the 38 uncapped on capacity you own. Escalate to the 61 for judgment only.
slides.source: Artificial Analysis, current Opus 5 vs Nemotron 3 Ultra comparison (blended $/M).
slides.notes: So what's the fix? Start with the trade, because it's concrete. The best US open-weight model against the frontier, on Artificial Analysis's own numbers. Smarter by a third: sixty-one to thirty-eight. Nearly seven times the price. Half the speed. That's not "open is as good." It's: most work doesn't need the sixty-one. A crane hired to hang a picture. The trade is the whole architecture: run the thirty-eight uncapped on capacity you own, and escalate to the sixty-one when the problem earns it.

slides.title: Three rungs you own, one gate you rent: routine stays inside, judgment escalates.

stats.l: US open on the rungs you own: $0.58 per million tokens, 100 a second, uncapped
the frontier, through one gate: $3.85 per million, 47 a second, metered
sensitive context stripped on the way out

slides.source: Artificial Analysis (index, price, speed). Token mix illustrative.
slides.notes: This is the sovereign ladder. Three rungs inside the fence. [advance] Device: the NPU laptops arriving with this refresh — AI-capable PCs pass half of shipments this year. [advance] Workgroup: a desktop inference box a team shares. [advance] Core: the racks, built later, out of the growth your natives create. [advance] And one gate: the only way out. Escalation to the frontier is earned, it's metered, and sensitive context is stripped on the way through. [advance] Two rules at once: volume is uncapped on the rungs, because the capacity is yours; escalation is earned, because that's where the meter and the leak live. Nobody should be picking models — the router does it.

slides.title: On a Tuesday, four pieces of an RFP stay inside. Two leave without the bid.
slides.notes: Here's what that looks like on an ordinary Tuesday. Someone drops in an RFP — pricing, technical response, capabilities, logistics — and asks what to do first. [advance] The router splits it. Four pieces land on your own rungs and get answered inside. Nothing about them ever leaves. The two hard questions — should we partner, what's the risk — need the outside world. [advance] Watch the gate: RFP number, deadline, bid — stripped, logged, policy-checked. [advance] The world sees a capability search. Options come back in, and a human makes the call. Only the boundary ever knew there was a bid. Don't build that router alone, and don't buy a dumb one — simple routers do not work. Use the open research.

slides.title: Past 5.3 hours a day, owning the box beats renting it.
slides.source: Lenovo 2026 TCO (vendor study): 5-year life, zero residual, 12% maintenance, $0.12/kWh; ~5.2-month break-even. Frontier and wrapped rates are Brad's reads.
slides.notes: Now the money. Same item, one million tokens of the same open model, four ways to buy it. Cloud GPU: ninety-seven cents. Frontier API at a blended coding rate: about twelve dollars. A wrapped federal LLM: up to forty-five. And owned capacity — whose price depends on one thing. [advance] At three hours a day, a dollar seventy-one. [advance] At five point three hours a day it matches cloud. That's the vendor study's break-even, about five months for an eight-GPU box. [advance] At twelve hours — a native's day — forty-three cents. The gap is utilization, not magic. Which is why you don't build this for everyone. You build it around the people who use it most.

slides.title: Find your one-in-a-thousand. In three months they'll have recruited their neighbours.

stats.l: people actually building their own agents on a harness
they burn more tokens than everyone else combined
of large enterprises say they're “scaling agents” — a count of deployments, not builders

slides.source: 1-in-1,000: Brad's field observation. 40%: McKinsey State of AI 2026. Spread illustrative.
slides.notes: Who keeps a box busy twelve hours a day? Inside real organizations, roughly one or two people in a thousand are building agents — not using one a vendor shipped, building their own. Call them the natives. Surveys say forty percent of large enterprises are "scaling agents"; that counts deployments. The builders are still one in a thousand. We are early. Thank god. [advance] Three months later, watch who gets red-pilled — always someone adjacent, demo by demo, team by team. Every new red stack is on the meter. Catch it while it's two dots and not fifty. Give them machines that are secured today and let them go. Everyone else in your industry is capping them. On owned capacity, you uncap. That's the weapon.

slides.title: Selling up the chain means sending each office the one sentence it can sign.
slides.source: The manifesto's three drivers — pricing, security, operations — translated per office.
slides.notes: Now the part you came for. Your leadership doesn't need the whole talk. Each office needs one sentence it can sign. [advance] The CFO: a cap costs more than capacity. Their problem isn't the size of the number; it's the detonation. Owned capacity is the predictable number. [advance] The CIO: IT rules for models. A curated model repository, a shim on every device, retrieval that follows the access controls you already have. The muscle IT already has, extended to models. [advance] The CEO: our decision graph is either our asset or their training data. [advance] Three tubes, three sentences. Don't send the CFO the CEO's sentence.

slides.title: Two numbers turn this talk into a purchase order: the burn map and utilization.

before.v: AI is a line item: seats, a subscription, a cap when it runs hot.

lever.v: Every system with an AI feature, who pays for its tokens, which model it calls, what breaks when that model is down.
Your natives' hours a day on the box. Above 5.3, capacity is cheaper than rent.

after.v: AI is capacity: a purchase with a payback date, sized to the people who burn the most.

slides.notes: Sentences get you the meeting. Numbers get you the purchase order. Bring two. First, the token-burn map: every system in the company with an AI feature in it, who pays for its tokens, which model it calls, and what happens when that model is down. Most of you can't answer the last column today — neither can your CIO, and that's your opening. Second, utilization: the hours a day your natives keep a box busy. That's the number that turns the vending machine into a payback date. Before, AI is a line item that gets capped. After, it's capacity with a break-even.

slides.title: Ask for it one refresh at a time: devices now, workgroup next, core when proven.

steps.v: An emergency refresh for the natives: secured, uncapped machines.
A shared workgroup box. The non-natives ride it.
The core, built out of the growth the natives create.
The frontier through one gate, metered, for judgment only.

slides.source: AI-capable PCs pass half of shipments in 2026 (Counterpoint). Power is the long pole: plan it now.
slides.notes: And don't ask for a datacenter. You can't put one down fast enough, and if you wait until the usage base is huge you can't afford the ten-megawatt facility your users need. So sequence it around the one-in-a-thousand. Now: an emergency refresh for your power users — don't wait for the cycle. Next: a workgroup box the rest share. The core gets built when the natives have proven it, out of the growth they create. And the frontier stays — through one gate, metered, for the hard calls. Prices are only going up and allocation is getting tighter. Power is the long pole. This isn't an IT ticket.

slides.title: The winners already run agents on a graph, with a human at the gate.
head: What they did
What it shows
rows: Agents for 90,000 employees; each picks its model; 80–90% of SEC-filing first drafts; primarily on-prem.
It works at scale — on their own iron.
12 agents per enterprise; half operate completely alone.
Ungoverned agents are the new shadow IT.
11% of planned agentic use cases reached production; an all-agent company hit 24% task success.
Loops fail. Graphs with a human at the gate don't.
slides.source: Fortune, Jul 2026; Salesforce 2026 Connectivity Benchmark; Futurum 1H 2026; CMU TheAgentCompany.
slides.notes: If someone upstairs says this is theoretical: Cisco put agents in front of ninety thousand employees this year. Each agent picks its model. AI writes eighty to ninety percent of the first draft of their SEC filing narratives. Primarily on-prem. Meanwhile the average enterprise runs twelve agents and half of them report to nobody — which is why only eleven percent of planned agentic projects reach production. The difference between the brain that works and the one that doesn't is the graph, and the human at the gate. Your business brain is the highest-intent object you'll ever own. Married to your data, it's double oil. Don't let it run on someone else's meter.

slides.title: By 2029 every organization has chosen, by acting or by not acting. Vote.

options.v: Uncap the natives on capacity you own, stand up the ladder, put a shim on every device.
Sign the renewal, cap the heavy users, trust the contract to cover traffic it never sees.

slides.notes: So here's the fork. By 2029 the capacity crunch, the renewals and the spikes have all arrived. The only variable left is the decision you make back here, now. Scan the code and vote — be honest about where your organization actually is, not where you'd like it to be. [wait 30–45 seconds; read the tally] Look at that split. That's the market. (Fallback if the code doesn't work: show of hands; the presenter presses 1 for own, 2 for rent.)

slides.title: Renting goes flat, flat, then vertical. Owning compounds.
rented: The renewal comes per user, in tiers. It isn't a dollar.
The natives hit the caps within a quarter; the side door does the rest.
By year four the spike reaches your industry: the routine 80% ships as someone else's feature.
Your best builders leave — some to build the thing aimed at you.
owned: The full ladder is standard: device, workgroup, core, gated frontier.
Enterprise agents with a registry, kill switches and a human at the gate.
The business brain runs on your rungs and never phones home.
Small teams outrun giants. The crew that wires the graph is the one everyone quotes.
slides.notes: Here's what each branch looks like. Rented: the renewal comes due per user, in tiers. The natives hit the caps in a quarter. The spend goes flat, flat, then vertical — and the caps didn't stop it, they moved it to the door the contract doesn't cover. By year four, the spike reaches your industry. Your experts are fine; experts always are. Your business model isn't. Owned: the ladder is standard, the agents have real guardrails, and your business brain compounds on your own rungs. And it's the moment small, fast teams outrun giants. Owning your own AI stops being a compliance chore and becomes the flex.

slides.title: Monday: uncap your natives on capacity you own, before the meter does it for you.

roles.v: Find the one-in-a-thousand. Arm them: secured, uncapped, on machines you own.
Build what you're exceptional at. Moat test: data they can't see, a relationship they can't have, judgment the 80% can't do.
IT rules for models: curated repos, device shims, retrieval that follows the ACLs. That's the unclaimed ground.

slides.notes: Three sentences for Monday, one per role. Owners: find your one-in-a-thousand and arm them, uncapped, on machines you own. Builders: build what you're exceptional at, and run the moat test before you ship — if you don't have data they can't see, a relationship they can't have, or judgment the routine eighty percent can't do, it's a feature waiting to be spiked. Operators: IT rules for models is the unclaimed ground. Nobody is building the policy layer under the router. Go build it.

slides.title: Intent is the new oil. Capping tokens is the leak.
slides.notes: The enemy isn't the lab you signed with — the router still sends your hardest calls to the best models in the world, and it should. The enemy is the default. The default plan trains. The default deployment meters. The default org caps its best people and then wonders where they went. Be the one who cut the leak. Thank you.
